title: Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 Sol on DeepSWE: Cost, Coding, and Routing
gist: On the DeepSWE coding benchmark (904 graded rollouts, 113 tasks), GPT-5.6 Sol wins single-shot quality (72.7% vs 68.5% pass@1) and reliability, but open-weight Kimi K3 pulls ahead at pass@4 (89.4% vs 85.8%) while costing 64% less per rollout; because the two models fail on different tasks (0.46 correlation), a Kimi-first cascade that escalates to Sol on test failure reaches ~85.6% accuracy, beating either model alone or a perfect one-shot router.

insights.claim: On the DeepSWE software-engineering benchmark, GPT-5.6 Sol beats Kimi K3 on a single attempt, scoring 72.7% pass@1 versus 68.5%, a 4.2-point gap, and this was described as the strongest single-shot score and highest reliability ever recorded on the benchmark at the time.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: For single-attempt, latency-sensitive coding tasks, Sol remains the higher-quality choice despite its higher price.
insights.quote: GPT-5.6 Sol took the pass@1 crown two weeks ago with 72.7% under DeepSWE's official scoring, the strongest single shot and the highest reliability ever recorded on the benchmark.
insights.locator: In our Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 Sol comparison on DeepSWE

insights.claim: As the number of attempts per task increases, Kimi K3 overtakes GPT-5.6 Sol: it wins pass@2 (82.0% vs 81.0%) and pass@4 (89.4% vs 85.8%), a 3.6-point lead at pass@4 that the article calls the best pass@4 of any flagship-tier model on the DeepSWE board.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: For retry-tolerant, high-volume agentic coding pipelines, Kimi K3's advantage compounds with more attempts, favoring it over Sol when latency per attempt is not the binding constraint.
insights.quote: At four attempts, Kimi's 89.4% beats Sol's 85.8% by 3.6 points, the best pass@4 of any flagship-tier config on the board.
insights.locator: The DeepSWE scoreboard: pass@1 and pass@k

insights.claim: The full analysis behind the comparison covered 904 graded rollouts across 113 DeepSWE tasks, with four trials per model per task, all run at max effort settings, using published per-trial records from deepswe.datacurve.ai.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: The sample size (113 tasks x 4 trials x 2 models) is large enough to support statistically meaningful routing/cascade conclusions rather than anecdotal comparison.
insights.quote: We analyzed all 904 graded rollouts (113 tasks, four trials each, at max effort on both sides) from the published per-trial records at deepswe.datacurve.ai.
insights.locator: In our Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 Sol comparison on DeepSWE

insights.claim: Kimi K3 costs $4.65 per DeepSWE rollout versus $8.37 for GPT-5.6 Sol, roughly 44% cheaper (a little over half the price), and delivers 14.7 solved tasks per $100 spent versus Sol's 5.3, about 2.8x more solved work per dollar.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: On a pure cost-per-solved-task basis Kimi K3 is a clear value pick for high-volume coding-agent workloads, making it the default choice unless single-shot reliability is paramount.
insights.quote: Kimi K3 delivers 14.7 solves per $100 versus Sol's 5.3, about 2.8x the work per dollar.
insights.locator: Cost comparison: Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 Sol pricing

insights.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol is far faster per attempt (median rollout of 17 minutes versus Kimi K3's 66 minutes) and uses roughly 40% fewer steps to reach an answer, so Kimi K3's cost and pass@k advantages come at the cost of latency, though the article expects end-to-end latency to improve as inference providers optimize serving of Kimi K3.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: Teams optimizing for wall-clock turnaround (e.g. interactive coding assistants) should weight Sol's speed advantage heavily even though Kimi K3 wins on cost and eventual accuracy.
insights.quote: The tradeoff is speed and steps: a median Sol rollout takes 17 minutes against Kimi's 66, with Sol using roughly 40% fewer steps.
insights.locator: Cost comparison: Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 Sol pricing

insights.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 occupy opposite corners of the coverage-vs-reliability plane: Sol achieves 84.5% reliability (61 of 113 tasks solved on all four tries) across 85.8% task coverage, while Kimi K3 reaches 89.4% coverage (widest of any flagship model) but only 76.6% reliability and 45 tasks solved four-for-four.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: Sol is the safer choice where determinism/consistency matters (e.g. CI gating), while Kimi K3 is better where broad task coverage across many retries matters more than per-attempt consistency.
insights.quote: Sol posts 84.5% reliability with 61 tasks solved four-for-four... Kimi K3 reaches 89.4% coverage, wider than any flagship, but only 76.6% reliability and 45 rock-solid tasks.
insights.locator: Coverage vs reliability: opposite corners of the plane

insights.claim: Kimi K3 and GPT-5.6 Sol solve different subsets of DeepSWE tasks (per-task correlation of only 0.46), in contrast to Kimi K3 versus a model called 'Fable', which the article describes as an 'echo chamber' with 0.72 correlation, meaning Kimi/Sol fail in genuinely different ways.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: Low correlation between two capable models is the precondition for profitable ensembling/routing; teams evaluating model pairs for a router should check task-level correlation, not just aggregate scores.
insights.quote: Where Kimi K3 versus Fable was essentially an echo chamber (0.72 correlation), Kimi K3 and Sol diverge: per-task correlation is 0.46.
insights.locator: How different are Kimi K3 and GPT-5.6 Sol?

insights.claim: Together, Kimi K3 and GPT-5.6 Sol solve 108 of 113 DeepSWE tasks (95.6%) at least once, which the article calls the best two-model portfolio coverage on the benchmark; the two models disagree on 18 of 113 tasks, and that disagreement is the exploitable surface for routing.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: 95.6% is presented as a hard ceiling for this two-model pair — squeezing further accuracy requires a third, differently-failing model rather than a better router.
insights.quote: Because the two disagree on 18 of 113 tasks, routing turns that disagreement into free accuracy.
insights.locator: How high can routing between them get you?

insights.claim: A verifier-gated cascade that runs Kimi K3 first and escalates to GPT-5.6 Sol only when the test suite rejects Kimi's result reaches about 85.6% accuracy at $7.30 per task — beating both a perfect one-shot oracle router (83.4%, ~$6.07/task) and running both models and keeping either (85.6% but $13.02/task) on cost.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: A cheap, verifier-gated cascade (cheap model first, escalate on failure) can beat a theoretically optimal single-shot router because it gives hard tasks two independent attempts instead of committing upfront — a reusable pattern for any multi-model coding-agent deployment with a test/verification harness.
insights.quote: The practical answer is about 85.6%: run Kimi K3 first and escalate to Sol only when the test suite rejects the result. That beats either model alone and even a perfect one-shot router (83.4%).
insights.locator: How high can routing between them get you?

insights.claim: The Kimi-first cascade is cheaper per solve than running Sol alone because Kimi K3 clears roughly 70% of the task queue on its own before Sol is ever invoked; without a verifier to catch bad answers, a realistic learned router only reaches accuracy in the 70s, well short of the 83.4% oracle ceiling.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: The routing/cascade gains described here are conditional on having an automated verifier (e.g. a test suite); teams without one should not expect to capture the 85.6% number and should budget for router accuracy in the 70s instead.
insights.quote: The verifier does the heavy lifting: without one, a realistic router lands in the 70s and 83.4% is the ceiling.
insights.locator: How high can routing between them get you?

insights.claim: Five of the 113 DeepSWE tasks are solved by neither Kimi K3 nor GPT-5.6 Sol across all eight combined attempts (four each), setting a hard 95.6% ceiling for this model pair that can only be raised by introducing a third, differently-failing model.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: Vendors selling multi-model routing/ensembling products should anticipate diminishing returns beyond two-model cascades and plan for three-way or N-way routing as the next lever for accuracy gains.
insights.quote: Past 95.6% you need a third model, not a better router.
insights.locator: How high can routing between them get you?

insights.claim: By programming language, Kimi K3 and GPT-5.6 Sol tie on Go (79-79); Sol leads Python (74-68), TypeScript (66-60), and JavaScript (75-65); Kimi K3 leads only Rust (65-60).
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: Teams with Python/TypeScript/JavaScript-heavy codebases should default to Sol for single-shot use, while Rust-heavy or Go-heavy shops see less differentiation or a Kimi K3 edge.
insights.quote: The two are tied on Go (79 each). Sol leads Python (74-68), TypeScript (66-60), and JavaScript (75-65). Kimi K3 takes Rust (65-60).
insights.locator: Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 Sol by programming language

insights.claim: By task domain, GPT-5.6 Sol leads 5 of 8 categories: serialization (92% vs 79%), concurrency (72% vs 55%), and program analysis (64% vs 56%) most decisively; Kimi K3 leads ops tooling (79% vs 73%) and runtime internals (77% vs 75%); conformance is roughly a coin-flip (61% vs 59%). Task types were classified by an LLM from each benchmark prompt.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: A domain-aware router (send concurrency/serialization/program-analysis tasks to Sol, ops-tooling/runtime-internals tasks to Kimi K3) could outperform a purely verifier-gated cascade, though this classification relied on LLM labeling rather than ground truth.
insights.quote: Send serialization (92-79), concurrency (72-55), and program analysis (64-56) to Sol. Send ops tooling (79-73) and runtime internals (77-75) to Kimi K3.
insights.locator: Where each wins, by task type

insights.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 fail differently: Sol breaks the repository's pre-existing tests in 20% of its failures (which the article says is consistent with other GPT models generally), whereas Kimi K3 breaks pre-existing tests in only 11% of failures but produces 'near misses' 65% of the time, where over 80% of new tests pass but a few still fail.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: Sol's higher rate of breaking existing tests is a regression-risk red flag for production CI pipelines even when it passes new-test checks, while Kimi K3's near-miss failures suggest it is often one small fix away from passing — useful signal for building targeted retry/repair loops per model.
insights.quote: Sol breaks the repo's existing tests in 20% of failures - this is pretty consistent with other GPT models actually. Kimi K3: 11% base tests failed but 65% near misses where > 80% new tests were passing but some failed!

insights.claim: Kimi K3 ships as an open-weight model (unlike GPT-5.6 Sol), which the article frames as the enabling factor for actually deploying the pass@4 gains, low cost, and Kimi-first cascade in production; Together AI positions its inference stack as built to serve open models like Kimi K3 at production scale without frontier per-token pricing.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: This is a vendor-interest data point: Together AI's own inference-hosting business benefits directly from teams choosing to run open-weight Kimi K3 rather than closed Sol, so the routing recommendation should be read with that commercial incentive in mind.
insights.quote: Kimi K3 ships as an open-weight model, which is what makes the pass@4 reach, the low cost, and the routing story above usable on your own terms.
insights.locator: Run Kimi K3 on Together AI

insights.claim: The Kimi K3 cost and timing figures were measured using the Kimi K3 API from Moonshot as of July 25th, meaning the specific dollar and latency figures cited reflect one provider/point-in-time snapshot rather than a stable, provider-independent baseline.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: Buyers should treat the $4.65/rollout and 66-minute figures as provider-specific and re-check pricing/latency across other Kimi K3 inference providers (including Together AI) since these numbers can shift as hosting is optimized.
insights.quote: using the Kimi K3 API from Moonshot as of July 25th
insights.locator: Cost comparison: Kimi K3 vs GPT-5.6 Sol pricing
